Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from Prof. Hajjar's lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Abdulrahman Alomar & Mohammed Alsalamah), every gift (red), and the Aldughaither summary (grey) at the end.

1. Introduction

  • The chest contains vital organs — damage to them threatens life.
  • Most common consequence is hypoxia.
  • Chest injuries cause a significant number of deaths each year: one in every 4 trauma deaths is caused by chest injury.
  • Injury can trigger a cascade from reversible physiological derangement to irreversible deterioration and death — one of the highest-yield systems in trauma assessment.

2. Mechanism of injury

  • 1) Blunt chest trauma — the most common cause of serious chest injuries. Post-RTA, falls, direct blows and crushing injuries. Many injuries are not immediately apparent on physical exam.
  • 2) Penetrating trauma — immediate result can be severe bleeding or impaired breathing. Any chest wound can involve underlying organ injury, no matter how superficial it looks. Injuries to the heart, lungs and great vessels can quickly lead to shock and cardiac arrest.
  • 3) Iatrogenic.
CategoryNotes
BluntMVCs, falls, direct blows, crush; internal injuries may be occult initially and declare themselves later
PenetratingStab or gunshot; severity depends on weapon size, velocity, distance, trajectory and number of wounds; unstable patients most often need exploration
Iatrogenice.g. subclavian central-line insertion → subclavian artery, lung or diaphragm injury → massive haemothorax/pneumothorax; uncommon but preventable
  • Force must pass through the chest wall (skin → muscle → ribs/sternum) to reach lungs, heart and great vessels — injury may be direct, compressive, or acceleration/deceleration. Sudden high-speed deceleration produces the greatest shear forces — the classic set-up for traumatic aortic injury.

High-speed road traffic collision · blunt steering-wheel injury to the chest

Penetrating injuries — impaled object and stab wounds of the chest wall

Chest X-ray of an impaled object · operative exploration

  • Never remove an impaled object in the ER — it may be tamponading an injured vessel or organ. Stabilize the patient and the object, and remove it under controlled conditions in the OR.
  • If the injury clearly needs exploration, image only if it will change immediate management. Alert anaesthesia and the specialties that may be needed (thoracic, cardiac, vascular, general surgery); cardiac injury may need cardiopulmonary bypass.
  • Pulseless on arrival after a penetrating (stab) wound of the anterior chest, lost the pulse in the ER / pulse 5 minutes ago → emergency (resuscitative) thoracotomy. 441 442
  • Sepsis patient 2 hours after a subclavian central line: tachycardia, falling BP and SpO₂ → tension pneumothorax (iatrogenic). 438 ×3
  • Transfusion of 2 L through a central line — the complication keyed → tension pneumothorax (from line insertion). 437

3. Signs, symptoms & assessment

  • Most common symptoms: pain and difficulty breathing.
  • Signs: obvious injury to the chest wall — look at both the front and back of the chest.
  • Note any subcutaneous emphysema (air under the skin).
  • Assessment: follow all steps of trauma assessment — primary survey (A Airway · B Breathing · C Circulation) → resuscitation → detailed secondary survey (CXR, ABG, ECG, CT chest, aortogram).

Trauma patient assessment — inspect the whole chest

Massive surgical (subcutaneous) emphysema of the face, neck and chest — crepitus on palpation

CXR and CT — air outlining the soft tissues and muscles (surgical emphysema)

  • Primary survey: airway + c-spine protection (assume a c-spine injury until proven otherwise) · breathing (inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate, RR, SpO₂, high-flow O₂) · circulation (BP, pulse, bleeding, bloods + crossmatch, fluids/blood). A patient who answers appropriately has, by definition, a patent airway. Always inspect the back during the log roll.
  • Do not delay transfer to a trauma centre or the OR for non-essential imaging — an unstable patient with a treatable cause goes straight to resuscitation and definitive management, not to CT/MRI.

Surgical (subcutaneous) emphysema

  • Air in the subcutaneous tissues → swelling with crepitus; may spread to the face, neck, even the groin; with or without a pneumothorax. CXR: air outlines the soft tissues and muscle fibres.
SourceMechanism (notes)
Respiratory (~85%)Rib fracture → lung/visceral pleural injury → air leak; post-op air leak (blocked/kinked chest tube), barotrauma (PPV/high PEEP), ventilated severe asthma. Massive or rapidly developing emphysema → exclude major tracheobronchial injury
Upper GI / oesophagealIatrogenic oesophageal perforation (endoscopy/dilatation, especially achalasia or cancer), duodenal perforation at ERCP, Boerhaave syndrome
  • Oesophageal rupture timeline: mediastinitis by ~4–6 h, severe by ~8 h, then sepsis and instability with very high mortality → early operative management, ideally within ~12 h.
  • Management: no single treatment — ABC + treat the cause; observe if stable and non-progressive. Urgent intervention if vital signs deteriorate or emphysema expands rapidly: chest tube ± suction (check any existing drain is patent); an extra tube for a large leak; bronchoscopy for massive unexplained emphysema after intubation; uncontrolled leak despite two chest tubes → thoracotomy.

4. Management principles

  • Ensure the patient has adequate oxygenation and perfusion.
  • Provide high-flow oxygen, ventilating when necessary.
  • Halt any obvious bleeding.
  • Support circulation when needed.
  • Rapidly transport the patient to definitive care.
Life-threatening — identified in the PRIMARY surveyPotentially lethal — found in the secondary survey
Airway obstructionTraumatic aortic rupture
Flail chestMyocardial contusion
Tension pneumothoraxTracheobronchial injury
Open pneumothoraxRuptured diaphragm
Massive haemothoraxOesophageal trauma
Cardiac tamponadePulmonary contusion
  • Immediately life-threatening injuries are treated as they are found; potentially lethal ones may emerge on the secondary survey (isolated traumatic oesophageal injury is very rare). Associated spinal or vascular injuries may coexist.
  • Rule out on the primary survey → open pneumothorax (not lung contusion, aortic disruption or diaphragm rupture — those are secondary-survey injuries). 431 ×3
  • Should be dealt with in the primary survey → massive haemothorax (aortic and oesophageal injuries are secondary-survey). 437

Tracheal or major bronchial rupture (notes)

  • Mostly blunt (very rarely iatrogenic). Dyspnoea, cyanosis, haemoptysis, crepitus, surgical emphysema, instability. X-ray: massive pneumothorax. A chest tube is inserted but the patient does not improve and the lung fails to re-expand → thoracotomy.

5. Rib fractures

  • Most common chest injury.
  • More common in adults than children; especially common in the elderly.
  • Ribs form rings — consider the possibility of a break in two places.
  • Most commonly the 5th to 9th ribs (poor protection).
  • Fractures of the 8th–12th ribs can damage underlying abdominal solid organs: liver, spleen, kidneys.
  • Fractures of the 1st and 2nd ribs require high force — frequently with injury to the aorta or bronchi; 30% will die.
  • Local swelling and tenderness may be the only sign; can be very painful; patients often present with guarding and shallow breathing.
  • Signs & symptoms: localized pain and tenderness that increases with coughing, moving or deep breathing · chest-wall instability · deformity, discoloration · associated pneumo- or haemothorax.
  • Management: move the patient carefully (bone ends can puncture the lung) · O₂ · allow self-splinting in the most comfortable position · limit movement · analgesia — morphine, PCA, epidural.

Chest X-rays — multiple rib fractures

  • Children's ribs are cartilaginous/compliant → fracture less often, but the compliant wall transmits force to the lung → more pulmonary contusion despite fewer fractures. Elderly → osteoporosis.
  • ~95% are treated conservatively. Analgesia is central: poor pain control → poor inspiration/cough → retained secretions → atelectasis → pneumonia (worst in the elderly, smokers, COPD/asthma).
  • Best analgesia: thoracic epidural (long-acting local anaesthetic such as bupivacaine ± fentanyl). Avoid a block that is too high — the diaphragm depends on the phrenic roots C3–C5 (mainly C4). Alternatives: PCA, IV opioids, local infiltration. Then deep breathing, coughing, incentive spirometry, physiotherapy, mobilization.
  • 80-year-old with 2 rib fractures after an MVA → admit and start pain control (elderly = high risk of pneumonia). 439

6. Flail chest

  • Flail segment: when three or more ribs are broken in two or more places, a rib-cage segment may detach from the rest — it is free floating.
  • Paradoxical movement: the flail segment moves in the opposite direction to the rest of the chest wall — can significantly impair breathing and injure the underlying lung.
  • Management: quickly stabilize the segment with a gloved hand; then a folded universal dressing taped securely over it; fixation (external, internal).

Flail segment — fractures of several adjacent ribs in two places; paradoxical movement

Chest X-rays of flail chest

Paradoxical movement — the flail segment moves IN on inspiration and OUT on expiration

Historical external fixation / traction of a flail segment

  • Positive-pressure ventilation ± paralysis can abolish or mask the paradoxical movement. Often coexists with pneumo-/haemothorax or pulmonary contusion.
  • Most are managed conservatively: excellent analgesia, physiotherapy, treat associated injuries, ventilate if needed. Ribs heal in about 4–6 weeks.
  • Indications for surgical rib fixation: severely displaced fractures · severe flail/paradoxical movement · bilateral flail chest · elderly/severe injury · significant lung disease (COPD) · failure to wean/extubate · already having a thoracotomy for another injury. Plates (titanium) — K-wire/traction techniques are obsolete.
  • Paradoxical chest-wall segment after a car accident → initial management: pain control and oxygen (not a chest tube, thoracotomy or fixation first). 442
  • True about flail chest → paradoxical breathing movement (it needs ≥ 3 ribs in ≥ 2 places, not 5; patients are symptomatic; thoracotomy is rarely needed). 438
  • Flail chest — the false statement: "management is usually by thoracotomy". 427

7. Post-traumatic pneumothorax

  • Types: 1) open pneumothorax · 2) closed pneumothorax.

Chest X-rays — traumatic pneumothorax (absent lung markings, visible lung edge)

CT showing pneumothorax · patient with a chest drain

  • CXR: absent peripheral lung markings, visible pleural/lung edge, increased lucency. CT is not routinely needed to diagnose an obvious pneumothorax.
  • Stable after an MVA, then mild left chest pain with hyper-resonance → traumatic pneumothorax (not primary — there is trauma; not tension — he is stable). 441
  • Minor fall, stable, mild SOB, mild pneumothorax → observation with supplemental oxygen. 442
  • Stable stab wound to the right chest, CXR: small pneumothorax + moderate effusion → chest tube. 439

Open pneumothorax

  • A sharp object penetrates the chest wall; if it has pierced the pleura, outside air can enter the thoracic cavity and the lung starts to collapse. Air in the pleural space = pneumothorax.
  • As air passes in and out of an open wound it can make a sucking sound — "sucking chest wound" means possible pneumothorax.
  • Signs: difficulty breathing, cyanosis, diminished breath sounds on the affected side.
  • Management: cover open chest wounds with an occlusive dressing (a gloved hand is an effective temporary one) · secure the dressing on three sides · high-flow O₂ · transport with the unaffected side slightly elevated.

Open (sucking) pneumothorax — chest-wall defect, collapsed lung, ball-valve effect on inspiration/expiration

Open chest-wall wounds

  • Pleural pressure is normally negative (≈ −6 to −12 mmHg), so air is sucked in through the wound — and may also enter from a lacerated lung. A valve-like wound can let air in but not out → tension pneumothorax within minutes.
  • 3-sided occlusive dressing (EXAM): tape 3 sides, leave 1 open — on inspiration it is sucked against the wound; on expiration the free edge lifts and lets air escape. As soon as possible: chest tube, cover the wound, definitive surgery as needed.
  • Open chest wound → 3-sided dressing. 431
  • Gunshot with a sucking chest wound, BP 70/30 → keyed initial step three-sided dressing. 434 ×2
  • Open penetrating left chest wound, laboured breathing, BP 100/70 → chest tube thoracostomy. 430

8. Tension pneumothorax

  • Build-up of pressure in the pleural space → fall in blood pressure. Potentially life-threatening — must be treated immediately. Can occur in blunt or penetrating trauma.
  • Mechanism: a one-way valve forms in the lung or chest wall → air enters the pleural space and cannot leave → pressure rises → lung collapses → trapped air pushes the heart and lung away from the injured side → both venae cavae become kinked → blood cannot return to the heart → cardiac output falls.
  • Signs: all those of a pneumothorax + JVD; if ventilating becomes more difficult, significant lung compression is indicated.
  • Signs & symptoms: extreme dyspnoea · restlessness, anxiety, agitation · decreased breath sounds · hyper-resonance · cyanosis · subcutaneous emphysema · rapid weak pulse · decreased BP · tracheal shift away from the injured side · jugular vein distension. Early dyspnoea/hypoxia — late shock.

Tension pneumothorax — rising intrapleural pressure, mediastinal shift, kinked venae cavae

X-rays and CT of tension pneumothorax — collapsed lung, mediastinal shift away

  • VERY IMPORTANT (classic OSCE): tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis — do not wait for a chest X-ray in an unstable patient. It causes both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, and develops especially fast on positive-pressure ventilation.
Needle decompression (notes)Detail
Site2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line
TechniqueAbove the rib (the neurovascular bundle runs below it); landmark: angle of Louis → 2nd costal cartilage
NeedleLarge-bore ≈ 12–14G (14–16G also discussed), ≈ 5–7.5 cm long (longer in a thick chest wall)
ConfirmationGush of air; remove the needle, leave the plastic cannula
PurposeBuys time — definitive treatment is a chest tube (tube thoracostomy)
The doctor (and every past key) uses the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line. The current ATLS (10th ed.) prefers the 4th–5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line in adults (thinner chest wall, fewer failures); the 2nd ICS MCL remains for children. For this exam, answer 2nd ICS MCL.
  • Typical tension picture (unstable, resonant, absent breath sounds, trachea shifted away) → tension pneumothorax 437; after an MVA with rib fracture, tracheal deviation and ↓ breath sounds → tension pneumothorax 439; motorbike crash, SpO₂ 85%, hypertympanic left chest, BP 80/40 → tension pneumothorax. 437
  • Tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock. 442 434
  • The sign that best separates tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade → breath sounds (absent in tension; both have hypotension and raised JVP). 438 ×3
  • First-line treatment → needle decompression, 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, then a chest tube. 432 ×3 436 429 428 442
  • Side matters: trachea deviated to the LEFT + absent breath sounds/hyper-resonance on the RIGHT → needle decompression on the RIGHT 2nd ICS MCL. 442 439
  • Intubated RTA patient, hard to bag, reduced air entry on the LEFT, trachea to the RIGHT → needle decompression on the LEFT 2nd ICS. 430
  • Stab wound with a picture of tension → needle chest decompression first. 433
  • MVA, hypotensive, reduced air entry on the right, ABG with hypoxia and respiratory acidosis → needle decompression (don't wait for an X-ray, don't intubate first). 434 ×2 431
  • During management of tension pneumothorax, the irrelevant step → confirming the chest tube with CT. 438

9. Haemothorax

  • Blood in the pleural space — the most common result of major chest-wall trauma; present in 70–80% of penetrating and major non-penetrating chest trauma.
  • Signs & symptoms: rapid weak pulse · cool clammy skin · restlessness, anxiety · thirst · chills · hypotension · collapsed neck veins.
  • Sources of bleeding: intercostal vessels · internal mammary vessels · lung parenchyma · bronchial arteries · major pulmonary vessels · heart and great vessels.
  • Management: secure the airway · high-concentration O₂ · rapid transport.
  • Indications for thoracotomy: initial output > 1250 mL · initial output > 1000 mL with hypotension · output > 250 mL/h for 3 hours.

Chest X-rays and CT — haemothorax (opacity, unlike the lucency of pneumothorax)

  • CXR: pleural blood = opacity. On CT look at the mediastinal/soft-tissue window as well as the lung window.
  • Notes' thresholds: massive initial drainage ≈ 1.5 L → urgent thoracotomy · lower output (500–600 mL) and stable → resuscitate and watch the tube closely · > 200–250 mL/h for 3 consecutive hours → OR. Goal: intervene before compensated haemorrhage becomes irreversible shock.
Thoracotomy threshold: the slide gives > 1250 mL initial (or > 1000 mL with hypotension) or > 250 mL/h × 3 h; the notes say ≈ 1.5 L or > 200–250 mL/h × 3 h; ATLS uses 1500 mL immediately or 200 mL/h for 2–4 h. All past keys (1600 mL, 1800 mL) are above every threshold.
  • Gunshot haemothorax, chest tube drains 1600 mL → emergent thoracotomy. 439 442
  • MVA haemothorax, 1800 mL immediately → urgent thoracotomy in the OR (an ED thoracotomy is for the arrested patient). 442
  • Stab wound to the right chest, BP 80/40, GCS 15 → chest tube insertion first (haemothorax — drain and measure). 438 ×5
  • Stab wound on the right side of the chest → initial step insert a chest tube. 434

10. Chest tube

  • Indicated to drain the contents of the pleural space — usually air or blood, but may be chyle or gastric/oesophageal contents.
  • Absolute indications: pneumothorax (tension, open or simple) · haemothorax · traumatic arrest (bilateral).
  • Relative indications: rib fractures + positive-pressure ventilation · profound hypoxia/hypotension + penetrating chest injury · profound hypoxia/hypotension + unilateral signs in a hemithorax.

Chest-tube insertion — landmark, incision, blunt dissection over the rib, finger sweep, tube in place

Drainage systems — one-, two- and three-bottle underwater-seal systems and a modern drainage unit

  • Ideal chest-tube site → 5th intercostal space (4th space above the 5th rib), mid-axillary line. 437 ×2 427
  • Landmark that finds the site quickly → level of the nipple (≈ 4th–5th ICS). 435
  • When inserting a chest tube → full aseptic technique. 436
  • Not an indication for a chest tube → pneumoperitoneum (chylothorax, pneumothorax and haemothorax are). 437

11. Pulmonary contusion

  • Bleeding into the lung itself. Bleeding and oedema impair gas exchange → hypoxia and respiratory failure.
  • Soft crackles may be heard over the injury; chest pain, point tenderness and swelling over the impact.
  • Management: support ventilation as needed · high-flow O₂ · transport to hospital (ventilation).

Chest-wall bruising · lung laceration at operation

Chest X-rays — patchy contusion opacities

  • Often with rib fractures, flail chest, haemo-/pneumothorax. Delayed presentation: changes can appear or worsen over hours (around 6–12 h).
  • Usually supportive; thoracotomy only for an associated injury (massive haemothorax, lung laceration from a rib).
  • Restrictive fluids: excess crystalloid leaks into the injured lung → worse oedema and oxygenation. Give only what keeps adequate intravascular volume (the lecture's example: ~80 kg patient, total crystalloid ≈ ≤ 1.5 L); blood/colloid stay intravascular better.

12. Diaphragmatic injury

  • Types: acute blunt injury · acute penetrating injury · chronic diaphragmatic hernia.

X-rays — bowel/stomach in the left chest, raised or lost hemidiaphragm, NG tube curling into the chest

CT — herniated stomach/bowel in the left hemithorax

Operative repair of the diaphragm

  • Trauma patient whose NG tube and stomach bubble are seen in the left chest → diaphragmatic rupture. 439

13. Cardiac contusion

  • Can impair the heart's ability to pump; bleeding into heart tissue → irregular beats. An irregular pulse should alert you to a possible cardiac contusion.
  • Diagnosis: fractured sternum · ECG: ST & T abnormality + dysrhythmias · CPK-MB.
  • Management: high-flow O₂ · ventilation support · circulation support · prompt transport · request ALS backup.

14. Pericardial tamponade

  • Bleeding into the pericardial sac compresses the heart — usually from penetrating trauma with laceration of the heart. Blood backs up.
  • JVD is a telltale sign; narrowed pulse pressure.
  • Management: high-flow O₂ · treat for shock · rapid transport to ER · request ALS · notify the hospital.

Precordial stab wound · cardiac laceration repaired at operation

  • Acute tamponade needs only ~100–200 mL of rapidly accumulated blood (chronic effusions are tolerated at much larger volumes).
  • Emergency pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid): enter ~1 cm below the xiphoid and 1 cm to the left, needle at ~45° aimed at the left shoulder tip, aspirate while advancing with monitoring — a temporizing manoeuvre.
  • (Notes also mention DPL — historically ~18G catheter; now largely replaced by FAST; decompress bladder and stomach first, aim toward the pelvis.)
  • Blunt chest injury with hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) → pericardiocentesis. 442 ×2
  • Penetrating chest wound with tamponade on eFAST → keyed emergency thoracotomy (surgical repair; pericardiocentesis only temporizes). 442
  • E-FAST cannot see retroperitoneal haemorrhage (it sees pericardial fluid, intraperitoneal blood and pneumothorax). 431

15. Aortic injury

  • In sudden deceleration (high-speed head-on MVCs) organs are thrown forcefully forward — the most significant tear is the aorta. A complete tear kills within minutes.
  • Management: high-flow O₂ · treat shock · rapid transport · notify the hospital.

Wide mediastinum (M/S ratio > 0.25–0.4)1st or 2nd rib fracture
Blurred aortic knobDepressed left mainstem bronchus
Pleural effusionBlunted AP window
Apical cappingHaemothorax, pneumothorax
NG tube deviationEnlargement of the paratracheal stripe

Blunt aortic injury — CXR signs; widened mediastinum

Aortograms — traumatic aortic tear / pseudoaneurysm at the isthmus

Operative repair of a traumatic aortic injury / emergency thoracotomy

  • Shear where the mobile arch meets the fixed descending aorta — the isthmus, distal to the left subclavian (ligamentum arteriosum). Intimal tear → false lumen/haematoma → may rupture; can be catastrophic or present later.
  • Definitive evaluation: CT angiography (aortography historically). Treatment has moved from open graft replacement to endovascular stent-grafting.

Conclusion

Decorative slide pictures (3)

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • Chest trauma ≈ 1 in 4 trauma deaths — blunt (most common), penetrating, iatrogenic.
  • Never remove an impaled object in the ER.
  • Tension pneumothorax is clinical — needle decompression (2nd ICS MCL, above the rib) immediately, then a chest tube.
  • 3-sided occlusive dressing for a sucking chest wound until a chest tube can be placed.
  • Haemothorax → thoracotomy at ≈ 1.5 L initial drainage or > 200–250 mL/h for 3 h.
  • 1st/2nd rib fractures = high energy (aorta, bronchus, great vessels); 8th–12th = liver, spleen, kidney.
  • Thoracic epidural is the best analgesia — poor pain control → atelectasis and pneumonia.
  • Aortic injury: deceleration → isthmus; widened mediastinum; CT angiography; stent-graft.
  • Flail chest = ≥ 3 adjacent ribs in ≥ 2 places with paradoxical movement; mostly conservative; know the fixation indications.
  • Pulmonary contusion: restrictive fluids; may appear 6–12 h later.

• Timely imaging (CTA, MRI) to detect vascular & spinal injuries.
  • Surgical repair of vascular, esophageal, & airway injuries.
  • High suspicion for BCVI in blunt trauma cases.
Thoracic Injuries:

Thoracic trauma contributes to 50% of trauma-related deaths due to its impact on airway, circulation, and respiratory function. Rapid identification and management of life-threatening conditions are crucial.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure and assess for tracheal injury, obstruction, or tension pneumothorax.
  • Breathing: Look for flail chest, pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion.
  • Circulation: Identify cardiac tamponade, aortic injury, or massive hemorrhage.
  • Disability (Neurologic): Monitor for spinal cord injury or hypoxia-induced brain dysfunction.
  • Exposure: Examine for penetrating wounds, bruising, subcutaneous emphysema.
Life-Threatening Thoracic Injuries (The “Deadly Six”):

1. Airway obstruction 2. Tension pneumothorax 3. Massive hemothorax 4. Flail chest 5. Open pneumothorax 6. Cardiac tamponade

Abdominal Trauma:

Abdominal trauma is categorized into penetrating and blunt injuries. Early identification and appropriate intervention are key to preventing shock, sepsis, and multiorgan failure.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure airway in unstable patients.
  • Breathing: Monitor for associated thoracic injuries.
